newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish air cargo rates mixed in holiday lull.
newsitem.headline: Swedish air cargo rates mixed in holiday lull.

text.p: Air cargo rates from Sweden were steady to higher as at least one foreign airline was forced to increase its rates because of a weaker crown and to protect income after the end of fuel surcharges, a Reuters poll shows.

However, traffic volumes have been depressed in May as Sweden celebrates three long weekends during the month and much business closes down, the survey of airlines and freight forwarders based at Stockholm's international Arlanda airport showed.

Still, most airlines and forwarders said they were busy, some pinning this to the effects of a weaker Swedish currency, which boosts Swedish exports, but other shippers said it was too early to reap the benefits from a depressed currency.
The crown has softened from 4.41 against the mark on December 17 and from 4.34 in October. It was trading at 4.48 against the mark at midday on Friday.
"The market seems to be fairly buoyant at the moment. The U.S. (market) seems to be creeping up at the moment," said Anders Uddman, cargo manager north Europe for British Airways.

"I presume it has to do with the currency situation -- the dollar is getting stronger so Swedish exports are cheaper. I think we will continue to see a boom unless the currency situation changes," Uddman said.
"When the market changes rapidly, players can't afford to use other methods of transportation. The sort of stuff we're flying now wouldn't normally be on an aircraft," he said.

The average market rate to New York from Stockholm rose to 10.10 crowns from 10 per kg/100 kg. To Chicago, the rate was 11.40 crowns compared to 11.30 at the time of the last ex-Stockholm market report and to Los Angeles it rose to 13 crowns from 12.90.
Lufthansa Cargo's Sven Ahlberg was equally optimistic about the traffic volumes.
"We have an all-time high every month from this office. This goes for us here in Stockholm -- southern and western Sweden have noted slower development," he said.
Par Wahlstedt, manager for cargo sales agent United Air Service AB, said there had been a few ad hoc shipments.
"During October and November there were no ad hoc shipments. Now there are some, but not many. We have quite a lot of cargo in the market and quite stable rates," he said.
Peter Sull, cargo and mail sales manager for the Nordic region for Thai Airways International, said the fact that there were many holidays in May did not affect rates.
"It's a little bit slow but not devastating. It doesn't rock rates because even if you lowered them there wouldn't be any cargo to have," Sull said.
Far Eastern cities continued to be named as the most important destinations from Sweden. Singapore Airlines cargo spokesman Bjorn Thun hinted traffic may be levelling out.
"I think the market is on its way up. It's more stable now -- it's not so much up and down," Thun said.

Rates were also slightly higher to the Far East, such as at 13.60 crowns per kg/100kg to Hong Kong versus 13.50 crowns and to Bangkok at 13.20 crowns versus 13.10. To Singapore the rate was steady at 13.60 crowns and to Tokyo it was nearly flat at 19.90 crowns.
The rate to Dubai was also marginally higher at 10.10 crowns compared to 10 crowns. To Johannesburg the rate was flat at 20.10 crowns.
Rates within Europe were unchanged at 7.45 crowns per kg to London and 7.25 crowns per kg to Paris.
To Sao Paulo the rate was also even at 20.70 crowns per kg.
"For us it's hard to find space to Argentina and Chile right now, if I compare with last year's figures," said one forwarder.
